source_text: Fortasse dicas mihi: quando ergo uenit a domino promissus paracletus? hic ego si non haberem aliud. quod crederem, facilius eum adhuc uenturum expectarem quam per Manichaeum uenisse concederem. nunc uero cum in actibus apostolorum manifestissime sancti spiritus praedicetur aduentus, quae me necessitas cogit haereticis tam periculose et tam facile credere? in libro enim memorato sic scriptum est: primum quidem sermonem fecimus de omnibus. o Theophile, quae coepit Iesus facere et docere in die, qua apostolos elegit per spiritum sanctum et praecepit praedicare euangelium. quibus praebuit se uiuum post passionem in multis argumentis dierum, uisus est eis per dies quadraginta et docens de regno dei, quomodo conuersatus sit cum illis et praeceperit eis, ne discederent ab Hierosolymis, sed sustinerent pollicitationem patris, quam audistis, inquit ex ore meo\' quoniam Iohannes quidem baptizauit aqua, uos autem spiritu sancto incipietis baptizari: quem et accepturi estis non post multos dies istos usque ad pentecosten. illi quidem cum uenissent, interrogabant eum dicentes: domine, si hoc in tempore repraesentaberis, et quando regnum Israhel. ille autem dixit: nemo potest cognoscere tempus, quod pater posuit in sua potestate; sed accipietis uirtutem spiritus sancti superuenientem in uos et eritis mihi testes apud Hierusalem et in tota Iudaea et Samaria et usque in totam terram. ecce habes, ubi commemorauit discipulos pollicitationis paternae, quam ex ore eius audierant de uenturo spiritu sancto. nunc uideamus, quando sit missus. paulo post enim sequitur et dicit: in illo tempore, quo subpletus est dies pentecostes, fuerunt omnes eadem animatione simul in unum; et factus est subito de caelo sonus, quasi ferretur flatus uehemens, et inpleuit totum illum locum, in quo erant sedentes; et uisae sunt illis linguae diuisae quasi ignis, qui et insedit super unumquemque illorum. et inpleti sunt omnes spiritu sancto et coeperunt loqui linguis, quomodo spiritus dabat eis pronuntiare. Hierosolymis autem fuerunt habitantes Iudaei, homines ex omni natione, quae est sub caelo. et cum facta esset uox, conlecta est turba et confusa est, quoniam audiebat unusquisque suo sermone et suis linguis loquentes eos. stupebant autem et admirabantur ad inuicem dicentes: nonne omnes, qui loquuntur, natione sunt Galilaei? et quomodo agnoscimus in illis sermonem, in quo nati sumus? Parthi, Medi, Elamitae et qui inhabitant Mesopotamiam. Armeniam et Cappadociam, Pontum. Asiam, Phrygiam et Pamphyliam, Aegyptum et regiones Africae, quae est ad Cyrenen; et qui aduenerant Romani et Iudaei incolae et Cretenses et Arabes audiebant loquentes illos suis linguis magnalia dei. stupebant autem et haesitabant ob id. quod factum est, dicentes: quidnam hoc uult esse? alii autem inridebant dicentes: hi musto omnes onerati sunt. ecce, ubi uenit spiritus sanctus. quid uultis amplius? si scripturis credendum est, cur non his potius credam, quae robustissima auctoritate firmatae sunt, quae cum ipso euangelio, ubi promissum sanctum spiritum pariter credimus, innotescere populis et commendari posteris praedicarique meruerunt? hos ergo actus apostolorum euangelio pari auctoritate coniunctos cum lego, inuenio non solum esse promissum illis ueris apostolis sanctum spiritum, sed etiam tam manifeste missum, ut nullus de hac re locus relinqueretur erroribus.
thought_title: The Holy Spirit's coming is proven from Acts
orientation: Augustine is answering a Manichaean objection that the Paraclete promised by the Lord has not yet come, by appealing to the Acts of the Apostles.
pass_a_gloss: Perhaps you will say to me: when then did the promised Paraclete come from the Lord? Here, if I did not have something else which I might believe, I would more easily expect him still to come than grant that he came through Mani. But now, since in the Acts of the Apostles the coming of the Holy Spirit is most clearly proclaimed, what necessity forces me to believe heretics so dangerously and so easily? For in the book mentioned it is written thus: 'Indeed we made the first discourse about all things, O Theophilus, which Jesus began to do and to teach on the day on which he chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the gospel. To whom he presented himself alive after the passion in many proofs of days, he was seen by them for forty days and teaching about the kingdom of God, how he had lived with them and had commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father, which you heard, he says, from my mouth. For John indeed baptized with water, but you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you are also about to receive not after many days, these days, until Pentecost.' They indeed, when they had come, were asking him, saying: 'Lord, if at this time you will be restored, and when will be the kingdom of Israel?' But he said: 'No one can know the time which the Father has placed in his own power; but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and even to the whole earth.' Behold, you have where he reminded the disciples of the Father's promise, which they had heard from his mouth about the Holy Spirit to come. Now let us see when he was sent. For a little later it follows and says: 'At that time, when the day of Pentecost was fulfilled, they were all with one accord together in one place; and suddenly there came from heaven a sound, as if a violent wind were borne along, and it filled that whole place in which they were sitting; and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it settled upon each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in tongues, as the Spirit was giving them to utter. But in Jerusalem there were dwelling Jews, men from every nation which is under heaven. And when this sound was made, the crowd gathered and was confused, because each one was hearing them speaking in his own language and in his own tongues. But they were astonished and were marveling to one another, saying: Are not all these who are speaking Galileans by nation? And how do we recognize in them the speech in which we were born? Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and those who inhabit Mesopotamia, Armenia and Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the regions of Africa which is toward Cyrene; and the Romans who had arrived and the Jewish residents and Cretans and Arabs were hearing them speaking in their own languages the great works of God. But they were astonished and were hesitating about this which had happened, saying: What does this want to be? But others were mocking, saying: These are all loaded with new wine.' Behold, where the Holy Spirit came. What more do you want? If the Scriptures are to be believed, why should I not rather believe these, which have been strengthened by the most robust authority, which together with the gospel itself, where we equally believe the Holy Spirit was promised, deserved to become known to the peoples and to be commended to posterity and to be proclaimed? Therefore when I read these Acts of the Apostles joined to the gospel with equal authority, I find not only that the Holy Spirit was promised to those true apostles, but also that he was so clearly sent, that no place for errors is left about this matter.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'Paraclete' for this term, not 'Advocate' or 'Comforter'.
Standard English rendering of the third person of the Trinity; the passage is about the promised Holy Spirit.
The standard English title for the biblical book; Augustine refers to it by this name.
Literal rendering preserving the genitive relationship; 'promise' is the key term for what was awaited.
Literal rendering of the mockery in Acts 2:13; 'loaded' preserves the image of being weighed down or filled.
Literal rendering preserving the superlative and the metaphor of strength; 'robust' matches the Latin 'robustissima'.

bible_refs.note: primum quidem sermonem fecimus de omnibus, o Theophile, quae coepit Iesus facere et docere... usque in totam terram
in illo tempore, quo subpletus est dies pentecostes... hi musto omnes onerati sunt

pass_b_english: Perhaps you will say to me: when, then, did the promised Paraclete come from the Lord? If I had nothing else to believe, I would more readily wait for him still to come than admit that he came through Mani. But as it is, since the coming of the Holy Spirit is proclaimed with complete clarity in the Acts of the Apostles, what necessity forces me to believe heretics so dangerously and so easily? For in that book it is written as follows: “In the first book, Theophilus, I dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach until the day when he chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the gospel. After his passion he presented himself alive to them by many proofs over a period of days, appearing to them during forty days and teaching about the kingdom of God. He stayed with them and commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, ‘which,’ he said, ‘you heard from my mouth; for John baptized with water, but you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you are also to receive not many days from now, until Pentecost.’ So when they had come together, they asked him, ‘Lord, will you be restored at this time, and when will the kingdom of Israel be?’ But he said, ‘No one can know the time that the Father has set by his own authority; but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth’” (Acts 1:1-8). Here you have the place where he reminded the disciples of the Father’s promise, which they had heard from his mouth about the coming of the Holy Spirit. Now let us see when he was sent. A little later the text continues and says: “When the day of Pentecost was fulfilled, they were all together in one place with one accord; and suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind rushing, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and settled upon each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance. Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And when this sound occurred, the crowd gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language. And they were amazed and astonished, saying to one another, ‘Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us, the language in which we were born? Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia, Armenia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, and the regions of Africa near Cyrene; and Romans who had come, and Jewish inhabitants, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them telling in our own languages the mighty works of God.’ And they were amazed and perplexed at what had happened, saying, ‘What does this mean?’ But others mocked and said, ‘They are all loaded with new wine’” (Acts 2:1-13). See where the Holy Spirit came. What more do you want? If the Scriptures are to be believed, why should I not rather believe these, which are confirmed by the most robust authority, which along with the gospel itself—where we equally believe the Holy Spirit was promised—deserved to become known to the peoples, to be commended to posterity, and to be preached? When I read these Acts of the Apostles, joined to the gospel with equal authority, I find not only that the Holy Spirit was promised to those true apostles, but also that he was sent so manifestly that no room was left for error on this matter.

last_rejected.why: Latin 'usque ad' means 'up to/until' but context shows Jesus spoke before Pentecost; 'not many days from now, until Pentecost' implies waiting until Pentecost, but 'usque ad' here means 'leading up to' or 'before' Pentecost occurs. The English 'until Pentecost' is ambiguous and could mislead.
last_rejected.fix: not many days from now, before Pentecost
last_rejected.ruling: 'usque ad pentecosten' naturally means 'until Pentecost'; the English faithfully renders the Latin. The claimed ambiguity is not a translation error.

last_rejected.why: Source says 'that whole place' (illum locum), not 'house.' The English adds 'house' which is interpretive and not in the Latin text.
last_rejected.fix: it filled that whole place where they were sitting
last_rejected.ruling: 'locum' can mean 'place, room, house'; 'house' is a legitimate rendering of 'illum locum' in this Pentecost context. Not a major error.

last_rejected.why: 'Eadem animatione' means 'with the same eagerness/spirit' (lit. 'same animation/soul'), not 'with one accord' which is a standard English rendering of ὁμοθυμαδόν but not what this Latin text says.
last_rejected.ruling: 'eadem animatione' = 'with same spirit/eagerness'; 'with one accord' is an acceptable equivalent. A preference, not a major mistranslation.

problems.quote: Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?
problems.source_quote: domine, si hoc in tempore repraesentaberis, et quando regnum Israhel.
problems.why: The Latin asks if he will be restored or present then, and when Israel’s kingdom will be, not if he will restore it.
problems.fix: Lord, will you be restored at this time, and when will the kingdom of Israel be?
problems.ruling: Source 'si hoc in tempore repraesentaberis, et quando regnum Israhel' is a garbled/different reading; 'restore the kingdom' is imported from Vulgate/Greek, not rendered from the Latin; misleads about the text.

problems.quote: visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes
problems.source_quote: qui aduenerant Romani et Iudaei incolae
problems.why: The Latin lists arriving Romans and Jewish inhabitants, not Roman visitors who are Jews and proselytes.
problems.fix: and Romans who had come, and Jewish inhabitants, and Cretans and Arabs
problems.ruling: 'Romani et Iudaei incolae' lists arriving Romans and Jewish residents; English 'visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes' adds 'proselytes' and changes the grouping.

edits.old: Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?
edits.new: Lord, will you be restored at this time, and when will the kingdom of Israel be?

edits.old: visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes
edits.new: Romans who had come, and Jewish inhabitants

fixed: Restored passive + added second clause per 'repraesentaberis, et quando regnum Israhel' — not 'restore the kingdom'.
Replaced Roman 'Jews and proselytes' with arriving Romans + Jewish inhabitants per 'qui aduenerant Romani et Iudaei incolae'.

last_rejected.quote: until the day when he chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the gospel
last_rejected.source_quote: quae coepit Iesus facere et docere in die, qua apostolos elegit per spiritum sanctum et praecepit praedicare euangelium
last_rejected.why: Latin in die means on the day, not until that day, so the first account’s scope is changed.
last_rejected.fix: We composed the first discourse, Theophilus, about all that Jesus began to do and teach on the day he chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit and commanded them to preach the gospel.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'in die, qua... elegit' means 'on the day'; English 'until the day' is the Vulgate-style Acts 1:2 sense ('usque in diem'), minor scope shift, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: we hear them telling in our own languages the mighty works of God
last_rejected.source_quote: audiebant loquentes illos suis linguis magnalia dei
last_rejected.why: Third-person narrator audiebant is turned into the crowd’s first-person speech.
last_rejected.fix: Romans who had come, Jewish inhabitants, Cretans and Arabs heard them speaking in their own languages the mighty works of God.
last_rejected.ruling: The crowd's speech continues in the Latin run-on ('audiebant loquentes illos'), and the first-person 'we hear' is a legitimate Acts 2:11 rendering; the meaning is preserved.

last_rejected.quote: will you be restored at this time
last_rejected.why: repraesentaberis means 'you will show yourself/appear' (present yourself). 'Be restored' is a different sense, likely imported from the Vulgate 'restitues'.
last_rejected.fix: ‘Lord, will you show yourself at this time, and when will the kingdom of Israel come?’
last_rejected.ruling: Later Latin repraesentaberis includes ‘be brought back/restored’; English follows that syntax, not Vulgate restitues.
